name: Isla Novak
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Isla' was chosen as an elegant, commanding name fitting her role as Zane's young but formidable mentor; the surname 'Novak' marks her as a member of the imperial Novak Family (source: the Su family's tie to the royal house and the Burning Sky Palace).
description: Isla Novak is Zane's martial arts master at the Skyreach Sect, only a few years older than her disciple, corresponding to Su Lingyun in the source novel. She claimed Zane as her disciple at his entrance examination (Ep 35) and trains him from Misty Peak, projecting a cold, regal authority that intimidates the other instructors. She belongs to the Novak Family, the same family as the emperor, which gives her standing even against figures like Saint Viana when Zane's life is on the line. Per the master sheet she is addressed as 'Master Novak' or 'Master Isla', never 'Missus' or 'Princess'. She remains a recurring presence across the Lower World arcs (Eps 35-1003).

name: Inner-Core Realm
reason: The source cultivation stage 'Divine Core Realm' was renamed 'Inner-Core Realm' to keep a concrete, body-centered image for the Western fantasy register while avoiding overuse of 'Divine' across tiers.
description: The Inner-Core Realm is a major cultivation realm above the Soul Realm, corresponding to the source's Divine Core Realm (early, mid and late stages are referenced, e.g. 'mid-stage of the Inner-Core Realm'). Warriors at this level are elite figures in the Lower World: stewards, sect experts and masters such as Kenneth and Cedric are placed here, and two Inner-Core warriors' combined mental assault can shatter an ordinary person's soul. Inner-Core masters can venture hundreds of miles into dangerous zones, though they rank below Spirit-Tribulation and Life-and-Death masters. It is one of the workhorse power tiers of Eps ~308-995.

name: Inner-Core Realm Zane
reason: Extraction artifact: a sentence fragment created by the realm name running into the name 'Zane' (2 occurrences, no coherent contexts); not a real entity.

name: Soul Sea
reason: The source stage 'Divine Sea (Realm)' was renamed 'Soul Sea' to tie the realm to the inner sea of power a warrior forms, fitting the adaptation's soul-based terminology. Verified against source chs ~1108-1111, where breaking through to the Divine Sea Realm liquefies a warrior's energy into an inner sea, exactly matching Ep 1130's 'truly created his Soul Sea'.
description: The Soul Sea is both an Upper World cultivation realm (the Soul Sea Realm) and the literal churning inner sea of power a warrior creates upon reaching it, after passing ten minor Heavenly Tribulations. It corresponds to the source's Divine Sea Realm. A potent Soul Sea can swallow even a Divine Weapon, and its waves churn whenever a warrior uses techniques; a Soul Sea nonetheless has its limits. Soul Sea warriors sit below Spirit Supreme figures but are a dominant power tier in the late arcs (Eps ~1118-1302).

name: Adrian
issues: Master sheet wrongly splits 'Adrian (Ep 263)' from Adrian Warrick: Ep 266 explicitly calls the Ep 263 tournament opponent 'Adrian Warrick... the pride of House Warrick', and both episode ranges map to the same source character Wang Yanmiao (chs 74-335; lotus techniques, Infernal/Purgatory encounter, pursuit of Zane's sister Elara = Luo Yan, confirmed ch 250). Masterls 'Caleb's brother' also conflicts with Ep 88's 'the only son and heir of House Warrick'. Separately, 'Adrian' mentions in Eps 1093-1143 belong to a different character, Adrian Rowe, and must not be merged into this one.
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Adrian' was chosen as a polished, aristocratic name fitting an elite noble prodigy; the surname 'Warrick' was assigned to his family, House Warrick, one of the Empire's Legacy Houses (source: the landowning Wang Family).
description: Adrian Warrick, heir of House Warrick (one of the most powerful Legacy Houses in the Empire), corresponds to Wang Yanmiao in the source novel. An elite Skyreach Sect inner disciple trained personally by the masters, he broke into the Soul Realm while his peers were still at the Nature Level, and fights with lotus-flower martial techniques. He courts Zane's sister Elara, which, together with an arrogant three-year challenge issued to Zane on Infernal Peak, makes him Zane's rival; dubbed 'Adrian the Arrogant', he makes a grand entrance at the All Peaks Competition (Ep 263) and is defeated by Zane (Eps 263-266). He first appears helping around Elara in Eps 88-99.

name: Adrian Rowe
issues: Shares the first name 'Adrian' with the earlier, unrelated Adrian Warrick (Eps 88-266); the two must remain separate entities.
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized: source 'Rao An' became 'Adrian Rowe', with 'Rowe' echoing the source surname 'Rao'.
description: Adrian Rowe (source: Rao An, ch ~1071) is a minor Upper World warrior at the seventh level of the Life-and-Death Realm, met during the group-stage battles against the Thirteen Palaces (Eps 1093-1095). Weak in cultivation but cunning and resourceful, his strategies earned his group several key victories, and he later probes after the secret treasure of the Dark World.

name: Lower World
reason: Source term 'Lower Realm' was localized as 'Lower World' for the Western fantasy setting, pairing naturally with 'Upper World'.
description: The Lower World is the mortal plane where Zane's story begins, corresponding to the source's Lower Realm(s). From the Upper World's perspective it is a backwater: ascenders from the Lower World ('Lower World runts') are looked down on, and power that could shatter a Lower World continent is commonplace above. Zane, and later other characters such as Christopher, ascend from it to the Upper World, and cities near the ascension gateways serve as waypoints stocked with Cultivation Methods for new arrivals. It remains a reference point for scale throughout Eps ~434-1320.

name: Sect
reason: Generic capitalized shorthand, not a distinct entity: in Eps ~11-500 'the Sect' refers to the Skyreach Sect (source: Blue Cloud Sect), already covered by its own entry, while later episodes use it for other sects; the bare common noun should not carry its own sheet row.

name: Elysian Keep
reason: The literal source term 'Immortal Mansion' was renamed 'Elysian Keep' to evoke a Western fantasy stronghold of a departed immortal rather than a Chinese xianxia 'mansion'.
description: The Elysian Keep is the ancient trial-filled stronghold of a long-dead Immortal, corresponding to the Immortal Mansion of the source novel (chs ~134+). Zane and other disciples become trapped inside it in Eps ~152-165, where it is shielded by a massive enchanted barrier and holds an imperial vault, the Tronson spear and the Tapestry of Sun Moon and Stars. Its guardian Saul (source: Afo) has waited roughly three thousand years for a successor, and the Immortal's inheritance test is designed so that someone far weaker than its maker can still inherit the Keep. It is referenced again across later episodes up to Ep 1320.

name: Dragon Scale
reason: Source term 'dragon scale' was kept literally as 'Dragon Scale(s)' since the image translates directly to the Western fantasy setting; the master sheet mandates two words, not 'Dragonscale'.
description: The Dragon Scales are the awakened draconic scales within Zane's body and mind, tied to the Cobalt Dragon (source: Qinglong) and appearing verbatim as 'dragon scale' in the source novel. Each awakened scale adds raw power: over a hundred scales can erupt at once, surging through Zane like liquid fire, and he channels their power into strikes such as his blows against the Earthen Armor; their glow (green in Ep 158) signals activation, though their power fades with use and consuming celestial essence does not always awaken new ones. The master sheet also records a related 'Copper Dragon Scale' artifact in Zane's mind (Ep 119) and 'Dragon Scale Shards' as a material (Eps 81-84). They are a signature power mechanic across Eps 24-1301.

name: Illusion Point
reason: The source's inconsistently translated scoring unit ('Fantasy Points'/'Illusory Points') was standardized as 'Illusion Points' to match the show's 'Illusion Battlefield' naming.
description: Illusion Points are the scoring currency of the Illusion Battlefield (Eps 1203-1321), corresponding to the source's Fantasy Points / Illusory Points. Competitors earn them by killing creatures and other warriors (a weak beast nets one or two, tougher kills ten or more), and the points are absorbed directly from slain foes. Death in the Battlefield is not final: the fallen are revived back in the city at the cost of half their Illusion Points, making point protection as important as point gain.

name: Patrick
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Patrick' was chosen as a steady, approachable name fitting his calm 'Inner Peace' temperament; no surname is used in the delivered episodes.
description: Patrick is the top-ranked active personal disciple of the Skyreach Sect ('the Sect's Chosen'), corresponding to Pei Tianyao in the source novel; only Evan (source: Li Yifeng), who skipped the tournament for secluded training, ranks above him. He trains under the philosophy of Inner Peace, making his mental calm his greatest asset, and wields golden-orb Cosmos techniques behind a gentle disposition that hides immense power. At the All Peaks Competition (Eps ~252-280) the sect's disciples look to him to salvage their reputation, setting up his clash with Zane.

name: Ethan Grant
issues: Known historical name drift: he was rendered 'Rory' in Eps 102-208 (localization error); 'Ethan Grant' is canonical per the show's decisions and the delivered episodes.
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Ethan' was chosen as a friendly, everyman name fitting Zane's cheerful companion, with the surname 'Grant'; his family became 'House Moon', echoing the source surname 'Mo'.
description: Ethan Grant is a Misty Peak pledge and one of Zane's closest friends at the Skyreach Sect, corresponding to Mo Can, the chatty youth who befriends Luo Zheng in the source novel. A self-described goofball from The Capital, he loves showing off his insider knowledge (such as explaining Celestial Essence to Zane) and little ever seems to get to him. In Ep 177 he is revealed as the heir of House Moon, a major power on the north side of the Capital. He accompanies Zane through the early sect arcs (Eps 29-250) and reappears as late as Ep 973.

name: Illusion Battlefield
reason: Source term 'Illusion Battlefield' (also rendered 'Illusory Battlefield' in the translation) was kept, standardized to a single spelling for the adaptation.
description: The Illusion Battlefield is a long-prophesied, periodically descending competition realm of the Upper World and the stage for the show's final arcs (Eps 1067-1321), matching the source's Illusion/Illusory Battlefield (chs ~1044-1310). Its opening is anticipated years in advance as a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and figures such as Layla and Lavender groom their champions specifically for it. Inside, warriors from the great races compete for rankings by accumulating Illusion Points, with death penalized by point loss and city revival rather than true death; its first stage is a pure point-ranking contest.

name: House Lowell
reason: The source's 'Luo Clan/Luo Family' was localized as 'House Lowell' to fit the Western noble-house register ('House', never 'Family' per the master sheet), with 'Lowell' echoing the surname 'Luo'.
description: House Lowell is Zane's family, a noble house corresponding to the Luo Clan of the source novel. It controls vast resources in Castermere County yet remains insignificant within the Eastern Territory's hierarchy, and once counted thirteen branches. Its signature martial style is the Purple Flash Fist, practiced for hundreds of years, and its well-trained young masters (such as the arrogant second young master Andrew) spar against the house's beaten-down slaves, which is where Zane's story begins. The house features heavily in the opening arcs (Eps 1-46) and is referenced through Ep 974.

name: Aether
issues: Possible merged term: the master sheet defines 'Aether Crystal' as a rare House Lowell heirloom (only two exist, Eps 2-90), but from Ep ~352 onward 'Aether crystals' are abundant, currency-like power stones (embedded in gateways by the dozen, traded in the hundreds of thousands) that map to the source's True Origin / True Essence Stones. One localized name appears to cover two different source items. Note per canon: standalone 'Vitality' (not 'Aether') is the energy; 'Aether Crystal' the item stays.

name: Layla Rhodes
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Layla' was chosen as a graceful name for a brilliant young prodigy, with the surname 'Rhodes'; her episode range (1059-1241) aligns almost exactly with source Ai Anxin's chapter range (1038-1221).
description: Layla Rhodes is a celebrated female genius of the Upper World, corresponding to Ai Anxin in the source novel (the confident prodigy who challenged all the geniuses of the Cloud Mist Heavenly Palace). Her fame draws a stream of challengers, and she fights alongside Zane through the arena group battles against the Thirteen Palaces, where their trials are deliberately made harder than anyone else's. At the Life-and-Death Realm she faces her Tenth Small Heavenly Tribulation while Zane still awaits his Sixth, and she is groomed as a key contender for the coming Illusion Battlefield.

name: Crown Prince
issues: Title with multiple referents, not one character: in Eps ~338-349 it is the Empire's Crown Prince in the Lower World (Saint Viana's brother, a pawn in succession politics against the Third and Seventh Princes), while in Eps ~783-903 it is the Crown Prince of a Divine Kingdom in a later arc. Mentions should not be attributed to a single person.
reason: Source title 'Crown Prince' was kept literally, as the Western term carries the identical meaning.
description: 'Crown Prince' is the heir-apparent title used across two arcs of the show, matching the source's own 'Crown Prince' (chs ~214-1136). The Lower World Empire's Crown Prince (Eps ~338-349) is a largely powerless but indispensable piece in the succession struggle among the princes, and is Saint Viana's brother, trapped by his fate. A later, different Crown Prince belongs to a Divine Kingdom arc (Eps ~783-903), where Zane pointedly refuses to kneel to him.

name: Crown of Destiny
reason: Source term 'Crown of Destiny' was kept literally; the term appears verbatim in the source chapters (~1145+).
description: The Crown of Destiny is the greatest prize in the universe and its most dangerous: the artifact without which even the most talented warrior cannot break past the World Lord realm (verbatim in the source, where a Heavenly Venerate's death releases a Crown back into the world). Its appearance always triggers a feeding frenzy among the great races, and no claimant can simply take one privately without every Supreme Lord hunting them down. Only a handful exist; the fourth was won by Lavender (source: Xun) with the help of the Dream God Arrow, and the Demon Night once chose one of their own to claim theirs. It drives the endgame conflict of Eps 1165-1302.

name: Crown
issues: Mostly the Crown of Destiny (all sampled contexts, Eps 1165-1199), but the entity's range starts at Ep 494, where 'Crown' more likely refers to the Heavenly Feather Crown (master sheet, Ep 492); a small share of the counts may belong to that separate item.

name: Crown Conduit
reason: The source's 'Baihui acupoint' (the acupoint at the crown of the head, tempered with golden light in ch 466) was reworked into the 'Crown Conduit', an energy channel containing 'Nexus Points', replacing Chinese acupuncture terminology with Western-fantasy anatomy.
description: The Crown Conduit is an energy channel in a cultivator's head containing twenty Nexus Points, which body refiners temper one by one with converging elemental forces; Zane ignites its first Nexus Point with golden light in Eps 478-479. It adapts the source's Baihui acupoint tempering, the first acupoint refined after crossing the Marrow Refining Realm.

name: Upper World
reason: Source term 'Upper Realm' (also rendered 'Upper World' in parts of the translation) was localized as 'Upper World', pairing with 'Lower World'.
description: The Upper World is the higher plane of existence to which Lower World cultivators ascend, corresponding to the source's Upper Realm / Upper World. It is a universe unto itself of staggering scale, holding complete stone inscriptions and cultivation methods unimaginable below, and its legends claim a person can only become a True God after abandoning all emotion. Even Dragon-blooded ascenders must pass a trial in a gateway city before truly entering, a culling that weeds out all but the most gifted; places like the Dragon Soar Arena are said to send winners straight up. It frames the entire second half of the show (Eps ~436-1321), where Zane arrives as a brand-new ascender.

name: Amber
reason: The character's Chinese name was fully localized to a US-origin name. 'Amber' was chosen as a warm, gem-like name for a gifted and kind-hearted woman; her episode range (589-1318) aligns almost exactly with source Liu Yu's chapter range (574-1298).
description: Amber corresponds to Liu Yu of the source novel, the super genius associated with the Demon Night race and the Heavenly Feather Holy Land from two hundred years back. She helped Zane more than once on the main continent before being held under the grasp of the Queen of Punishment (source: the King who controlled punishment), and her friend Aurora once spoke in hushed fury of trying to free her. In the late-war episodes she fights on the front line beside a tall Demon Night woman, steadying the exhausted Aurora with calm reassurance. She recurs across Eps 589-1318 with a strongly female pronoun signal, matching the source.
